planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in spring, or divide established clumps before new growth resumes.

directions: Anna Marie is a classic montbretia selection carrying bold orange-red, trumpet-shaped flowers on arching sprays above pleated, sword-like foliage from midsummer into early autumn, and has been offered for decades by UK specialty bulb growers such as Jacques Amand International. Plant corms about 4 inches deep in well-drained, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, where established clumps multiply steadily by cormlets. It tolerates light shade but flowers most heavily in full sun, and the nodding blooms draw hummingbirds and make a long-lasting cut flower. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep flowering vigorous.

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in well-drained, organically rich soil in spring; avoid strongly alkaline ground.

directions: Disco Dancer produces unusually large flowers in bright orange suffused with gold, carried on wiry, branching stems above strappy, pleated foliage, and is sold by UK bulb specialists including Jacques Amand International as one of the larger-flowered montbretia selections. Give it full sun and well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, planting corms roughly 4 inches deep in spring; it struggles in heavy, alkaline ground, so improve drainage before planting on clay. Left undisturbed, clumps bulk up quickly from cormlets and reward with a long midsummer-to-late-summer bloom season that holds up well as a cut flower. Lift and divide only once flowering begins to decline, usually after three or four seasons.

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in an open, sunny, well-drained site in spring.

directions: Emberglow carries large, glowing orange-red flowers with a contrasting yellow throat, a combination that sets it apart from more uniformly colored older montbretia hybrids, and it is classed among the large-flowered Crocosmia selections offered by UK bulb nurseries. Plant corms about 4 inches deep in an open, sunny position with well-drained soil, since waterlogged winter ground is the most common cause of losses. Clumps increase steadily from cormlets if left undisturbed for several seasons, producing ever more flower spikes in mid- to late summer. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting, and divide only once flowering starts to thin out.

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in free-draining, non-alkaline soil in spring.

directions: Firestarter bears yellow flowers rimmed with a fine red edge that outlines each petal, a bicolor pattern that reads almost painted from a distance, and it is offered by UK specialty growers as a distinct montbretia introduction. Grow it in full sun with tolerance for light shade, in free-draining soil that is not strongly alkaline, planting corms around 4 inches deep in spring. The wiry flower spikes open over a long midsummer window and cut well for indoor arrangements, while the clump bulks up from cormlets if left in place for a few years. Mulch over the corms in the colder part of its range to protect against hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil in spring; avoid strongly alkaline ground.

directions: Hotspot carries sunny yellow flowers with a sharply contrasting cherry-red center, held on taller stems than many montbretia cultivars, and is marketed by UK bulb specialists as an Award of Garden Merit-level garden performer. Plant corms roughly 4 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding strongly alkaline ground where it performs poorly; established clumps naturalize readily if left undisturbed for several years. The extra height and vivid bicolor flowers make it a strong vertical accent toward the back of a mixed border, and spikes cut well for indoor display. Divide congested clumps in early spring once flowering begins to decline.

planting.note: Plant corms about 4 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil in spring; stake or interplant for support given its height.

directions: Scorchio produces orange-yellow flowers streaked with red down the center of each petal, among the tallest named montbretia selections, and is marketed by UK bulb specialists as an Award of Garden Merit-level garden performer. Plant corms about 4 inches deep in full sun in well-drained soil, since it tolerates only light shade and dislikes strongly alkaline conditions. Because of its height, stake it or interplant with sturdy neighbors to keep the flower spikes from leaning in wind and rain. Left undisturbed for several seasons, clumps multiply readily from cormlets and the fiery blooms remain a strong draw for hummingbirds and a good cut flower.

planting.note: Plant corms about 2 inches deep in autumn in free-draining, sandy soil in full sun to very light shade.

directions: Burtonii is a naturally occurring sport of Freesia alba that arose in New Zealand and has since become one of the most widely naturalized freesias there, prized for creamy yellow flowers that lack the purple flush typically marking the uppermost petal of the species. Plant corms about 2 inches deep in autumn in free-draining, sandy soil in full sun to very light shade, where it tolerates winter wet far better than many South African bulbs. Once established, it seeds and multiplies freely along roadsides, dunes, and open ground in mild climates, so site it where some spread is welcome. The strongly fragrant flowers open on wiry stems in late winter to spring and make an excellent, long-lasting cut flower.

common_name: Sara Nobles Freesia (Large Deep-Mauve Freesia laxa Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.

directions: Sara Nobles is a deliberate hybrid between Freesia laxa subspecies azurea and subspecies laxa, documented by Pacific Bulb Society growers, combining the two into a plant substantially larger than either parent, with deep mauve flowers that stand out from the species' more common scarlet-red or white-and-red forms. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, planting corms 2 to 3 inches deep in spring where winters stay above about 15 degrees F. Grassy, iris-like foliage emerges in late winter ahead of loose sprays of flowers carried into early summer, and established corms offset readily into a spreading patch. Divide clumps after several years if flowering declines, replanting offsets immediately into refreshed soil.
